Matias

I suspect the problem comes from a misunderstanding about the units of measure.  Before thinking about detection functions and model selection, let me just check whether I understand your study in general terms.

From what you have described in your data, your study area is about 21 hectares, correct?  The total length of your 15 transects is 67.19km (correct)?  You truncated your detections to 0.6km (600m).  Therefore the size of the covered area (area surveyed by your survey) is

67.19 x 0.6 x 2 (because you looked on both sides of the transect) = 80.6km^2

This seems implausible to me because your study area is 0.21km^2.  This means you examined your study area 400 times over. 

The story makes more sense if your study area is 21km^2 because this would result in an abundance estimate on the order of 84 animals within the 21km^2, translating to a density of roughly 4 animals per km^2.

I'm not guanaco expert, you'll have to tell me which of the above is true.  Please double check your units and let us know which is correct.

Hola Matias,
I work with guanacos in Patagonia too. I agree with Professor Rexstad in that you may need to check/adjust the units of the measurements that you entered when you imported the data (I presume this just by looking at your email). Also, check/use english notation for numbers (just points -no commas- for decimals) before you try to import the data again.

If data table is all the data there is, you have 147.56 km of transect length, x 0.6km x 2sides = 177.07 km2 of covered area. 

Other thing that you may need to look at is the number of observations. You have few observations in the data table. You may need more than 60-80 groups for a "decent" model. You can achieve this by increasing the effort in the field by increasing the number of transects (say 20 or more), or the length of transects (by extending transects or repeating transects within days).

Matias

Thanks for sending along your Distance project as a zip file.  I am not understanding the size of your study area.  One square kilometer is 100 hectares, so if you say your study area is 21.486ha, then it is actually 0.21486 km^2. 

Googling a random guanaco survey publication
Schroeder, Natalia M., Silvia D. Matteucci, Pablo G. Moreno, Pablo Gregorio, Ramiro Ovejero, Paula Taraborelli, and Pablo D. Carmanchahi. 2014. ‘Spatial and Seasonal Dynamic of Abundance and Distribution of Guanaco and Livestock: Insights from Using Density Surface and Null Models’. PLOS ONE 9 (1): e85960. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0085960.

That publication shows guanaco densities in their study area to be 3 - 20 animals per km^2.  That would be on the order of 0.6 - 4.2 animals per 21.486ha.  Therefore the estimate of 1.0 produced by Distance is not implausible.  Furthermore because there is large variability in number of detections between transects, and large variability in detected group sizes, the uncertainty in the estimate has the confidence interval between 0 and 1 (because Distance forces abundance estimates to be integers).

With such a small study area for an animal occurring at such low densities, perhaps it is better to examine the estimated density of animals labelled as (D) in the output.  This estimate is 0.0337 animals per hectare.  Convert this estimate to density per square kilometer (by multiplying by 100) we get 3.37 animals per square kilometer, which is in the range reported by Schroeder et al. (2014), with a confidence interval of 1.7 to 6.8 animals per sq. kilometer.

My argument is based upon your study area size to be 21.486ha, which seems quite small for animals occurring at such low densities.  Correct me if I am wrong about any of this.
